pg007_p005: Food additives are added to food to bring the desired effects by making it safe and palatable to consumers. They should be used as specified to prevent health hazards. In this chapter, you will learn about the concept of food additives, the guidelines for using food additives and categories of food additives. The competence developed will enable you to appropriately use food additives in preparing appealing dishes.
pg007_p014: Food with or without food additives
pg007_p016: Food additives are substances added to food to enhance its flavour, appearance, texture, and extend its shelf life. They can be natural or synthetic. Food additives do not provide nutrients, but they are added to the food to serve different technological functions including preservation, colouring, and improving the appearance and taste of food. They are normally added when food is prepared and eventually become a component of the food.
pg007_p023: For an additive to be acceptable for use it must meet the following conditions.
pg007_p025: Must be safe to use: Food additives should not pose any health risks when consumed.
pg007_p027: (ii) Must be used as intended: Food additives should be used specifically for
pg007_p028: their intended purpose in the food.
pg008_p003: (iii) Must be used in required amounts: Food additives must be used according to
pg008_p004: their specifications. The correct amount of it should be used in food.
pg008_p005: (iv) Must meet the technological justification: The additives must have a valid
pg008_p006: technological function such as preservation, flavour enhancement or colour retention.
pg008_p008: (v) Must be compatible: Food additives must be chemically and physically
pg008_p009: compatible with the food and other ingredients.
pg008_p011: Food additives are categorised according to their intended use. They include food colouring agents, preservatives, stabilizers, thickeners, flavour enhancers, artificial sweeteners, emulsifiers, antioxidants, anticaking agents and glazing agents.
pg008_p015: Food colouring agents are substances used to enhance the visual appeal of food by adding or restoring colour. They are normally used to restore, impart or enhance colour to the food. Food colouring agents are found in liquid or powdered form and can be natural (derived from plants or animals) or artificial (synthetically produced).
pg008_p019: Examples of natural colouring agents include beetroot extract (red) chlorophylls
pg008_p020: (green), turmeric (yellow) and beta-carotene (orange/yellow). Artificial food colours are chemically produced and they are more stable compared to the natural ones, which means the colour will remain vibrant and consistent over time, even when exposed to factors like heat, light, or air. They are of different colours including red, yellow and blue. Despite their benefits, some food additives may cause allergic reactions, intolerance or sensitivities in certain individuals. Overuse or long term consumption of synthetic additives can pose health risks such as cancer and toxicity in liver and kidney. pg009_p016: These are substances added to food to prevent spoilage caused by microorganisms like bacteria, mould and yeast or chemical changes like oxidation. Preservatives are added to products primarily to extend their shelf life. They ensure that the food remains fresh and appealing for longer periods. Additionally, preservatives play a crucial role in preventing food borne illnesses by inhibiting the development of pathogens that can cause diseases. Excessive use of preservatives may cause allergic reactions to some individuals. Preservatives are commonly used in food products like jams, juices, canned foods and baked goods. There are two types of preservatives
pg010_p003: namely natural and synthetic. Natural preservatives include salt, sugar, vinegar and spices such as cloves and cinnamon. Synthetic preservatives are laboratory made chemicals such as benzoates, sorbates, and sulphites.
pg010_p007: These are food additives used to maintain or improve the texture, consistency and appearance of food products.
pg010_p009: Stabilisers: They help in maintaining uniform distribution of ingredients and prevent their separation during storage. Commonly used stabilisers include lecithin and pectin. Some compounds such as xanthan gum and pectin can function as both thickeners and stabilisers.
pg010_p013: Thickeners: They work by increasing product viscosity without affecting its taste.
pg010_p014: Thickeners help in improving mouthfeel and overall texture. They are commonly used in soups, sauces, gravies and yoghurt. Examples of thickeners include cornstarch, pectin and gelatine. These substances absorb water and swell to form a gel or thick consistency.
pg010_p019: Flavourings are substances added to food to enhance or modify its natural taste and aroma. They make the food more palatable and appealing to consumers hence increasing consumers’ acceptance. It also allows for greater product variety. They can either be natural or synthetic. Natural flavourings are natural extracts from foods.
pg010_p023: An example of natural flavouring includes vanilla extract. Synthetic flavourings are chemically synthesized. An example of this flavouring includes ethyl vanillin.
pg010_p025: Synthetic flavourings are extracts which come from different sources including animal products and aromatic plants such as vanilla, lemons, pineapples, cloves and peppermint. Flavourings are widely used in a variety of products such as sweet snacks, soft drinks and sauces such as caramel sauce and chocolate sauce. However, some synthetic flavourings may cause allergic reactions or sensitivities in certain individuals. Figure 1.3 shows different food flavourings.

pg011_p017: Spices: These are aromatic parts of plants which include roots, barks, leaves, flowers and seeds. They have distinctive aroma and pungent flavours. They are added to foods to improve flavour, aroma and appearance. Most of them are used in whole or ground form. All spices should be stored in airtight containers to prevent flavour loss. pg023_p019: Cereals represent a fundamental component of the human diet across many communities thus serving as a principal source of nutrients and energy. When consumed, they provide important nutrients that support the overall health and proper functioning of the body. In this chapter, you will learn about the concept of cereals, types of cereals, uses and methods of cooking cereals. You will also learn about cereal products. The competencies developed will enable you to prepare, cook and serve dishes using cereals as well as to earn money from selling cereal products.
pg023_p006: Cereals are edible seeds or grains of cultivated grasses. They are staple foods in many regions in Tanzania and in other parts of the world. Cereals are easy to grow, transport, prepare and cook. They are also non-perishable; hence, they can be stored for a long period without spoiling. They are useful for making human diets, brewing purposes and feeding livestock. Well dried whole-grain cereals should be kept in tightly covered containers and stored in cool, dry places to prevent mould growth and pest infestation. Stored cereals should be inspected regularly to check if there is any sign of infestation for appropriate measures to be taken.
pg023_p015: There are different types of cereals. These include wheat, rice, maize, sorghum, finger millet, oats, barley and pearl millet. Figure 2.1 shows different types of cereals.
pg024_p011: Wheat grain is generally oval shape. It is brown on the outside and white on the inside. Wheat grain contains various nutrients distributed on its different parts.
pg024_p013: The endosperm is rich in starch and protein. The bran contains large quantities of dietary fibre; B vitamins such as B1, B2, B3, B6, and folate; small amount of minerals including iron, magnesium, zinc, phosphorus, copper and manganese. The Germ is the embryo or sprouting part of wheat grain. It contains a small amount of protein and a greater share of B vitamins, lipids and trace minerals. The Aleurone is a thin layer between the bran and the endosperm while Scutellum is also a thin layer between the germ and the endosperm. Both layers contain high amounts of B vitamins. The protein substance present in wheat is known as gluten. It causes stretching of dough when water is added to the wheat flour.

pg025_p017: Rice is a cylindrical grain obtained through milling of paddy. It is particularly rich in starch on the endosperm. Compared to other cereal grains, rice contains the lowest levels of dietary fibre and protein. It provides a moderate amount of fat and B vitamins such as vitamin B1 (Thiamine), and vitamin B3 (Niacin). Essential minerals like magnesium and phosphorous are primarily located in the outer layers of the grain. The germ is rich in protein, lipids, and vitamins including vitamin E and several B vitamins.
pg025_p024: Rice is mainly categorised based on the processing method, with the main categories being polished and unpolished rice.
pg025_p026: Polished rice: This type of rice is highly milled to remove the outer layers such as husk and bran, resulting in a smooth, white grain. This process removes most of the nutrients like protein, minerals, vitamins and fat that are concentrated in the outer layers thus making polished rice less nutritious than unpolished (brown) rice.
pg025_p030: However, it is preferred by many due to its appealing taste, soft texture and ease of digestion. Parboiled rice is a type of polished rice that is partially cooked with its husk to prevent nutrient loss from the grains. This is done by soaking the paddy in cold water for a day and then steaming, drying and milling it. Soaking enables
pg026_p003: the endosperm to absorb nutrients such as proteins, vitamins and minerals from the bran. As a result, the nutrients remain inside the grain during milling. This type of rice is firm, and it can be stored for a long time due to its thorough drying process.
pg026_p006: Sometimes it has an unpleasant smell and an unappealing colour.
pg026_p007: Unpolished rice: This type of rice does not undergo extensive milling as a result, the bran and germ rich in B vitamins, minerals and protein remain intact. This type of rice has a dull brown colour. It is commonly referred to as brown rice or whole grain rice and it is more nutritious. However, it is less commonly consumed due to the unpalatable texture of the bran. Additionally, unpolished rice has a shorter shelf life because the fat content in the germ is susceptible to oxidation over time.

pg026_p020: Sorghum grains are typically small, round with a slightly flattened or elliptical shape. Their colour varies by variety, ranging from white to red, brown or even black. Sorghum is a drought-tolerant crop and versatile cereal grain. It is rich in carbohydrates, mainly starch. It is a good source of dietary fibre and protein.
pg026_p024: Additionally, sorghum provides essential minerals like potassium and B vitamins such as thiamine and niacin.
pg026_p027: Millet is a small round generally tiny grain. The most widely grown millet in Tanzania includes finger millet and pearl millet. Their plants can withstand harsh climatic factors such as unpredictable climate and they can flourish in nutrient-depleted soils. Thus, they are considered resilient in difficult climatic conditions. Millet is a good source of carbohydrates and protein. The essential amino acid profile of millet protein is better than that of other cereals such as maize. Millet is also rich in calcium, phosphorous, magnesium, vitamin E, K and B3 (Niacin).
pg027_p004: Maize grains are typically large compared to other grains like rice, millet and sorghum. The grains are generally oval to round, featuring a flattened inner side. The exact shape may vary depending on the maize variety and kernel type. The colour of the kernels can range from yellow, white, red and purple. Maize, also known as corn, is a good source of energy in the form of starch. Yellow corn is a good source of carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A upon consumption. However, niacin in maize is mostly found in a bound form, making it less readily absorbed by the body. Maize is widely cultivated due to its adaptability to different environments, high yield potential, and multiple uses. pg028_p029: Most cereals can be processed into a variety of products. The most common product derived from the milling of cereals is flour. Other cereal-products include breakfast cereals such as rice flakes made from rice and cornflakes made from maize. Likewise, wheat is used to produce products like pasta, noodles and semolina.
pg029_p004: Flour is the powder obtained by milling or grinding cereals such as wheat, sorghum, maize, millet and rice. It can be categorised based on the degree of processing method and its gluten content.
pg029_p007: Category of flour according to the degree of processing method
pg029_p008: In this category, there are two types of flour based on the degree of processing. namely wholemeal flour and white flour.
pg029_p011: This type of flour is made by grinding the entire grain, including the bran, germ and endosperm. It is darker in colour and more nutritious than refined flour because it contains all parts of the grain. A good example is non-dehulled maize flour.
pg029_p015: Wholemeal flour has the following advantages.
pg029_p016: High in nutrients: Wholemeal flour delivers all nutrients found in whole grains.
pg029_p017: These include B vitamins, particularly niacin and thiamine, and minerals such as zinc, iron, magnesium and manganese.
pg029_p019: High in fibre: Being rich in dietary fibre, meals made from this flour help a person to feel full thus preventing overeating. Likewise, the fibre in whole grains supports healthy digestion by adding bulk to stool and lowering the risk of constipation. It also slows down the absorption of sugar into the blood stream, making it beneficial to people with diabetes.
pg029_p024: Lower energy density: Wholemeal flour has a lower energy density compared to refined flour, which may help to reduce the risk of overweight and obesity.
pg029_p026: Consequently, consuming wholemeal flour can lower the risk of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as heart disease and high blood pressure.
pg029_p028: Pleasant flavour: The flour gives a pleasant nutty flavour to baked products.
pg029_p030: The following are the disadvantages of wholemeal flour.
pg029_p031: It cannot be stored for a long time. This type of flour has a higher fat content than white flour thus increasing the risk of oxidation and rancidity which limits its shelf life.
pg030_p003: It contains antinutrients that reduce nutrient absorption. Wholemeal flour contains antinutrients, which are naturally occurring compounds in foods that can interfere with the absorption or utilisation of nutrients, potentially reducing their nutritional value. For example, phytic acid, commonly found in cereals, may impair the absorption of minerals such as zinc, calcium, and iron by forming insoluble compounds with them.
pg030_p009: It affects the quality of certain baked products. It does not produce good-quality baked products, particularly for items like cakes and pastries. The high fibre content in this flour interferes with gluten development and it affects texture, often resulting in denser, less tender baked goods with reduced volume.
pg030_p013: It is more susceptible to mycotoxin contamination. Mycotoxins are naturally occurring toxic substances produced by fungus. In cereals, mycotoxins tend to be mostly concentrated in the bran. Therefore, wholemeal flour is more susceptible to contamination by mycotoxins because it is processed by using unrefined cereals.
pg030_p017: Poor storage conditions remain the major cause of fungal contamination hence increasing the risk of mycotoxin contamination in cereals. If consumed in amounts exceeding safe limits, they can lead to adverse health effects such as acute poisoning.
pg030_p020: Proper handling and storage of cereals are essential to minimize this risk.
pg030_p022: White flour is also known as polished flour. It is highly milled and sieved to remove the outer layers (bran) and germ. Approximately 30 per cent of the grain, mainly the bran and germ, is removed during milling. Hence, only 70 percent of the original grain remains. White flour lacks essential nutrients such as calcium, iron, B vitamins, zinc, niacin, copper and magnesium, which are predominantly found in the bran and germ that are removed during milling. Fortification can be applied in the refined flour to restore the missing nutrients.
pg030_p030: The following are the advantages of white flour.
pg030_p031: It has improved baking qualities. White flour derived from wheat has improved baking qualities. It produces baked products with a fine texture and light appearance thus making it ideal for breads, cakes and pastry dishes.
pg030_p034: It contains reduced quantities of antinutrients. This flour has fewer antinutritional compounds such as phytic acid, which are mostly removed during refining hence nutrients absorption in this type of flour is easier.
pg031_p003: It can be stored for a long time. White flour contains less fat hence it does not undergo rancidity that change the flavour of products.
pg031_p005: It is less susceptible to mycotoxin contamination. Mycotoxins tend to be mostly concentrated in the bran, which is removed in the process of producing white flour.
pg031_p007: White flour is processed by using refined cereals.
pg031_p009: The following are the disadvantages of white flour.
pg031_p010: Insufficient nutrients: During milling, white flour loses essential nutrients such as protein, B-vitamins and minerals such as calcium and iron.
pg031_p012: Low dietary fibre: White flour has readily available sugar due to low fibre content.
pg031_p013: When one consumes white flour, the sugar present is rapidly absorbed, contributing to overweight and obesity. Likewise, white flour increases the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
pg031_p016: Increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases: Consuming large amounts of white flour can lead to overweight and obesity which increases the risk of heart diseases since most of the fibre for slowing down the absorption of sugar is reduced during milling.
pg031_p020: Lower bowel movement: Dietary fibre helps to regulate bowel movement. In contrast, white flour contains very low quantities of dietary fibre; thus, it increases the chances of constipation.
pg031_p023: Other types of flour obtained from either whole grain or white flour include self- rising flour, enriched flour, germ flour and semolina. These are described as follows.
pg031_p026: Self-rising flour is a type of flour that already contains a baking powder thus eliminating the need for additional raising agents in baking. It is typically made from refined white wheat flour. A common formulation involves mixing 6 g of baking powder with 125 g of wheat flour, whose ratio is approximately 1:21 to give a sufficient raising action. Self-rising flour is suitable for making plain cakes and scones.
pg032_p004: Enriched flour is the one made by adding specific nutrients to it. These nutrients include B vitamins such as vitamin B1 (Thiamine), vitamin B2 (Riboflavin), vitamin
pg032_p006: B3 (Niacin) and vitamin B9 (folic acid), and minerals like iron that are lost during the milling process.
pg032_p009: Germ flour is made by mixing white flour and germ in a ratio of 3:1. Wheat germ is normally baked before being added to the flour to stop the action of enzymes and prevent fat rancidity. Cooking the germ gives the flour a malted nutty flavour. This type of flour cannot be stored for a long time due to the presence of fat which tends to oxidise easily.
pg032_p015: Semolina is a coarse flour made from durum wheat, a hard variety of wheat that contains more protein and gluten. It is different from the common wheat used in regular flours. Semolina has a pale yellow colour, attributed to its richness in carotenoids. Nutritionally, semolina is high in complex carbohydrates, protein, and essential minerals such as iron and magnesium.
pg032_p020: There are various grades of semolina based on texture. Coarse semolina is primarily used to make pasta while fine semolina is commonly used in making desserts, porridges, and baked goods. Bakers also use semolina in bread, pizza crusts, and cakes to enhance texture. Semolina is a valuable plant-based source of protein and iron, making it particularly important in vegetarian and vegan diets. However, because it contains gluten, it is not suitable for individuals with gluten intolerance or celiac disease. When stored in a cool, dry place in an airtight container, semolina has a relatively long shelf life and it is less prone to spoilage compared to whole wheat flour.
pg032_p029: Pasta is produced by mixing durum wheat semolina with water to form a stiff dough, which is then kneaded to develop gluten. The dough is shaped by extrusion or rolling and cutting, depending on the desired type of pasta. For dried pasta, the shaped dough is carefully dried under controlled conditions to reduce moisture content and ensure long shelf life. Fresh pasta skips the drying stage and is usually consumed shortly after preparation. There are different types of pasta, including macaroni, spaghetti, couscous and vermicelli, each varying in shape and culinary application. Spaghetti is the most familiar pasta; it is long, thin, solid, cylindrical pasta. Vermicelli is a very
pg033_p003: thin, long and rounded pasta. Apart from wheat, vermicelli can also be made from rice and it is known as rice vermicelli or rice noodles. Figure 2.2 shows different types of pasta.

pg033_p015: Category of flour according to the amount of gluten
pg033_p016: Gluten is a protein primarily found in wheat. It is also available in some other cereals in very small quantities. The strength of the flour is determined by the amount of gluten it contains. Based on the amount of gluten, wheat flour can be categorised into three types, strong flour, medium flour and soft flour.
pg033_p021: Strong flour has a high gluten content between 12 and 14 percent. This amount of gluten makes the dough more elastic and lighter, resulting in an airier texture product during baking. It is also known as bread flour. This type of flour is normally used to make bread, buns and dinner rolls. Strong flour can be converted to soft flour
pg034_p003: by adding corn flour in the ratio of 2:1, meaning that the amount of strong flour is twice the amount of corn flour.
pg034_p006: This type of flour has less gluten content between 9 and 12 percent. It is appropriate for household baking needs such as bread, pizza, cookies, plain biscuits, scones and pastry dishes. It can also be used as thickening agents for sauces. This type of flour includes all-purpose flour and pastry flour.
pg034_p011: This type of flour has low gluten content, ranging from 7 to 9 percent. It is milled in a fine texture. Soft flour is also known as cake flour because it is suitable for making soft textured products like cakes and pastry.

pg035_p028: Cereals can be prepared using a variety of cooking methods. Most of them are easy to apply. Each method has an impact on the final texture, flavour and nutritional quality of the cereal dish prepared. Most cereals, such as rice, are cooked by boiling.
pg035_p031: Other methods include baking, frying and pressure cooking. For example, rice is partially cooked by boiling and then simmering it until it is fully cooked. Pressure cooking can be used for cooking foods that are hard to cook like maize and kidney bean dish. Baking can also be used, especially in preparing wheat based products like bread and buns while frying is often employed in the preparation of food items such as buns, chapati, doughnuts, and cereal-based fritters.
pg036_p004: Baking is a method of cooking in the hot dry air of a heated oven. The food should be baked at the right temperature to cook the inside part without hardening the outer surface. This method is suitable for cooking foods that have more moisture such as cakes, biscuits, puddings and breads. Likewise, some foods may sometimes be covered during baking in order to keep them moist, for example, casserole dishes.
pg036_p010: To achieve the best results during baking, the following rules should be adhered to:
pg036_p012: (i) Preheat the oven to the right temperature before placing food in.
pg036_p013: (ii) Put the food on the right shelf because the top shelf is the hottest and the middle and lower shelves are moderately hot.
pg036_p015: (iii) Observe the recommended baking time for specific items being baked.
pg036_p016: (iv) Do not open the oven before the flour mixture sets to avoid letting in cool air as it will make the mixture sink.
pg036_p018: (v) Test baked foods for readiness before removing them from the oven.
pg036_p019: (vi) Do not overcrowd the oven to ensure proper air circulation and even baking.
pg036_p020: (vii) Do not shut the oven door hardly as it can make the baked food sink into the centre.

pg050_p010: Batter is a mixture of flour, liquid and eggs. Rice and wheat flour can be used. The liquid may include water, milk or coconut milk. Eggs in the batter play the roles of binding, trapping air and enriching the mixture. In making batter, the mixture should be beaten well to smoothen it and incorporate air as a raising agent. Besides beating, air can be incorporated into the batter through sieving the flour. The trapped air expands when the mixture is heated. These raising agents give a light texture to the food after cooking. The methods used in cooking batter dishes include baking and frying. Baked batter dishes are light and digestible. Furthermore, the steam produced during the cooking process acts as a raising agent. Other kinds of raising agents such as baking powder and yeast may also be added, depending on the type of dishes to be prepared. For example, bhajia, rice buns and banana fritters use baking powder as a raising agent.
pg050_p023: The types of batter depend on the consistency of the mixture. This consistency depends on the amount of liquid used in making the batter. The mixture should be covered and allowed to stand for at least ten minutes in a cool place for the liquid to be absorbed by the starch granules before using it. There are three types of batter, namely thin, medium or coating and thick batter, which is also known as fritter batter.
pg050_p029: Thin batter: This type of batter is used to make food dishes like pancakes, pancake sachet, Yorkshire pudding and toad in the hole. It is also used to bind foods such as samosas as well as to thicken sauces and stews.

qz004_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! Herbs are added to dishes to improve their flavour, aroma, and appearance.

qz030_o1_exp: ❌ Not correct. The text explains that fluids help regulate body temperature and prevent dehydration, not reduce sleep.

qz032_o2_exp: ✅ Correct! A lactating mother needs extra fluids because breast milk is mostly water, so fluids help maintain an adequate milk supply.
